transcript.text: Indesit dryer making a horrible squealing noise when it starts up, goes away after a few mins. Still dries fine

A squeal on start-up that fades after a few minutes is a very common tumble dryer fault. It's usually a worn part that is noisy when cold and quietens as it warms up and loosens. It won't damage anything immediately, but it typically gets worse, so it's worth sorting.

## Most likely causes (roughly in order)

1. Jockey wheel / idler pulley: This spring-loaded pulley keeps the drive belt tight. Its bearing dries out and squeals, especially when cold. It's very common on Indesits.
2. Drive belt: An old, glazed or stretched belt can slip and squeal on start-up, when the drum (plus wet laundry) is hardest to turn. Look for black rubber dust inside the machine.
3. Drum support rollers / rear drum bearing: These wear and cause squeaking or rumbling. They're often sold as a kit for Indesit dryers.
4. Drum felt seals: If worn, the metal drum rubs on the casing. This sounds more like a scraping squeak, and you may see fluff or a dark mark around the drum edge.
5. Motor bearings: These are less common. If the motor itself is squealing, it's usually a whole-motor replacement.

## Quick checks you can do

• Turn the drum by hand (machine off, door open). Does it squeak, feel rough, or catch? Then it's probably the rollers, bearing or seals.
• Run it empty. If the noise is much quieter, the belt or tensioner is struggling under load.
• Listen for where it's coming from. Noise from the bottom front or middle usually means the jockey wheel or motor. Noise from the back usually means the rear bearing or rollers.

## Fixing it

• Unplug it first. If it's a condenser model, empty the water tank.
• On most Indesits, the top lid and then the front panel come off with a few screws. This gives access to the belt, jockey wheel and front rollers.
• Parts are cheap: a belt is roughly £10–20, a jockey wheel £5–15, and a roller/bearing kit £15–30. Search using the model number on the sticker inside the door.
• If you're replacing the belt, do the jockey wheel at the same time (and the rollers if the drum is out). It's the same job and saves doing it twice.
• Don't spray WD-40 on the belt or pulleys. It may quieten things briefly but makes the belt slip and attracts fluff.
• While it's open, hoover out the lint inside the casing. Built-up fluff is a fire risk.

## When to call someone

If the drum is hard to turn, you smell burning, or it starts grinding or knocking rather than squealing, stop using it. A local repairer would typically charge £60–120 for a belt, pulley or roller job.

If you tell me the model number (on the inside of the door or rim), I can point you to the likely parts and how to get the panels off.

The model is IDC8T3B. I turned the drum by hand with it unplugged and it turns, but there's a slight squeak/scrape and it feels a little rough. The noise is worse with a heavy load. It seems to come from low down, front or back, I can't tell which.

That's useful. The roughness when turning by hand narrows it down, but with the belt still on you're also turning the motor and jockey wheel, so it could still be any of them. The way to pin it down is to take the belt off and test each part on its own. This takes about 20–30 minutes.

## Why "low down" matters

• Jockey wheel and motor sit low at the bottom of the machine. These are prime suspects.
• Front drum supports (felt seal and plastic slides/pads, depending on the exact build) are at the lower front, where the drum's weight rests.
• Rear drum bearing is usually at the centre of the back panel, not low down. A bad one also tends to rumble or let the drum move up and down.

Worse under heavy load fits a dry jockey wheel bearing, a slipping belt, or worn front supports.

## Getting the belt off

1. Unplug it and empty the water tank.
2. Remove the top lid. On most Indesits there are 2 screws at the back. Slide it back and lift.
3. Remove the front panel. Take out the kickstrip/plinth at the bottom if fitted, then the screws along the top and bottom. Lift the panel slightly and pull it forward. Photograph the door switch wiring before unplugging it.
4. You should now see the drum, the belt, and underneath it the motor pulley and jockey wheel.
5. Push the jockey wheel against its spring to slacken the belt, then slip the belt off the motor pulley.

## Testing each part

• Drum alone (belt off): Turn it by hand. If it still squeaks, scrapes or feels rough, it's the drum supports or bearing. If it's now smooth and silent, the problem is underneath.
• Jockey wheel: Spin it with your finger. It should be smooth and quiet. If it's gritty, noisy, wobbly, or has a flat or grooved surface, replace it. This is the most common culprit.
• Motor pulley: Turn it by hand. If it feels gritty or has play, the motor bearings are going.
• Belt: Look for cracks, a shiny glazed surface, fraying, or black rubber dust in the base.
• Front of drum: Check the felt seal for thin or missing patches, and the slides/pads for wear. Bare metal or shiny rub marks on the drum lip are a giveaway.

## Parts

Search the model number IDC8T3B on a parts site (e.g. eSpares, Partmaster or Hotpoint/Indesit's own service site). The exact drum support setup varies by production version, so check against the full model/serial number on the sticker inside the door.

• Jockey wheel: about £5–15. Replace it with the belt if they're both old.
• Belt: about £10–20.
• Drum support kit (seals, slides, bearing): about £15–30.
• Motor: much more expensive, often £60+. Worth confirming before buying.

If you tell me what you find with the belt off, I can point you to the right part and the fiddly bits of fitting it. The belt can be awkward to get back on, but there's a knack to it.
I haven't taken the panels off. I've only got basic tools and a bad back, so I can't tilt or lift it. Is there anything I can check without taking it apart, or is this a job for a repairer?

Yes, there are a few useful checks you can do without tools or lifting. They won't always give a definite answer, but they'll help a repairer get to it faster.

## Checks you can do standing or sitting

1. Look at the front edge of the drum (use a torch)
Open the door and look around the rim where the drum meets the front of the machine.
• Black marks, shiny rub marks, or bits of torn felt or fluff suggest the front felt seal or drum supports are worn. This fits the scrape you felt.
• If it looks clean and even, the noise is more likely underneath (jockey wheel, belt or motor).

2. Check for drum play
With the machine unplugged, put your hands inside the drum near the front and gently lift it up and down, then push it side to side. A small amount of movement is normal. Noticeable clunking or sagging points to worn front supports or a rear bearing.

3. Check for black dust
Look around the door seal, the filter area and the floor around the base. Black rubber dust means the belt is wearing or slipping.

4. Check it isn't rubbing on something
Make sure the dryer isn't touching a wall, cupboard or worktop, and that it isn't rocking on its feet. It sounds too simple, but vibration against a neighbouring surface can squeal.

5. Record the noise
Start a cold run and record on your phone, held first near the bottom front, then near the back. Playing it back often makes the location clearer. It's also very useful to show a repairer.

## Things to avoid
• Don't spray WD-40 or oil through gaps. It can get on the belt and make it slip worse, and it's not something you want near the heater.
• Don't overload it in the meantime. Smaller loads reduce strain on the belt and jockey wheel.

## Is it a repairer job?
Honestly, with a bad back, yes. Getting the front panel off means working low down near the floor, and the fix itself involves crouching and reaching under the drum. It's not hard for someone who does it every day.

Rough UK costs:
• An independent repairer is typically around £70–£130 including labour, plus parts. The parts are cheap (often £20–£40 for a belt, jockey wheel and roller/support kit).
• A new equivalent condenser dryer is roughly £250–£350, so repair is usually worth it unless the machine is very old.

Tips when booking:
• Give them the model (IDC8T3B) and describe what you've found: squeal on start-up that fades, worse with heavy loads, slight rough scrape turning by hand, noise from low down.
• Ask them to replace the belt and jockey wheel together and check the front drum supports while it's open. It's cheap to do it all in one visit.

## Is it safe to keep using for now?
Generally yes, short term. Stop using it if:
• the squeal becomes constant or much louder,
• you smell burning, or
• the drum stops turning or turns jerkily.
